156-061.r: Podzol → soil of coniferous (Taiga) forests of Eurasia and North America.

156-062.r: Mocha coffee → Yemen; named after the Mocha seaport from where it was exported.

156-063.r: Not in tea → morphine; tea has theanine, caffeine, tannin, polyphenols, theobromine, theophylline.

156-064.r: Agreement on Agriculture Green Box → support for agricultural research and plant protection (pest and disease control), training and extension; not fertilizer or irrigation.

156-065.r: Incorrect: sugarcane as Malaysia's major plantation crop; Malaysia → rubber. Correct: cocoa → Ghana; coffee → Brazil; tea → Sri Lanka.

156-067.r: Golden Crescent (illicit opium area, Central and South Asia) → Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan; not Iraq.
156-067.h: Golden Crescent = AIP: Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan.

156-068.r: Maize as staple food → Middle Africa.

156-069.r: Sacramento–San Joaquin Valley (Central Valley) → California, USA; famous for citrus fruit production.

156-070.r: Commercial viticulture → Mediterranean Europe, because 85% of its grapes go to wine making (A and R true, R explains A).

156-071.r: Citrus fruits → well developed in Mediterranean regions (subtropical dry-summer climate).

156-072.r: High-yielding variety seeds first developed → Mexico, by American agronomist Norman E. Borlaug.

156-073.r: Catechu → obtained from the wood of the Khair tree (Acacia catechu).

156-074.r: Peanuts (groundnut) → main crop of Gambia among options; Ghana now produces most of these; China is the largest producer globally (FAO 2023).

156-075.r: Native place of groundnut → Brazil (Mato Grosso area, South America).

156-076.r: Shahtoosh shawl wool → hair of the Tibetan antelope (Chiru), found almost entirely in China (Tibet, Xinjiang, Qinghai); a few in Ladakh, India.

156-079.r: Viticulture → science of growing grapes; when grapes go to wine making, viniculture; a branch of horticulture.

156-080.r: Wrong pair: vegetable cultivation – horticulture; vegetables → olericulture. Correct: flowers → floriculture; crops → agronomy; fruits → pomology.

156-081.r: Silk production → India ranks second, after China (FAO 2023).

156-083.r: Australia rears cattle more for meat than milk (about 2.2 of 30.1 million for dairy, 2025); Australians are traditionally non-vegetarian (A, R true; R explains A).

156-084.r: Largest livestock population → China (829.58 million, 2020), then India, Brazil, USA (FAO).

156-085.r: Mad cow disease → destroyed beef's safe image in Europe and America; first broke out in 1986 in the U.K.

156-086.r: Largest milk producer → India (247.87 million tonnes in 2024-25, NDDB; 485 grams per person per day); then USA, Pakistan, China, Brazil (2023 data).

156-088.r: Highest milk yield per cow among options → Denmark (100283 hg/cow, FAO 2020), ahead of Netherlands, Great Britain, India; Israel highest overall.

156-089.r: Milk producers, descending (2011): India > USA > China > Russia; Yearbook 2025: India, USA, Pakistan, China, Brazil.

156-090.r: Second largest corn (maize) producer → China, after USA; Brazil third (FAO 2023).

156-091.r: 'Sugar Bowl of the world' → Cuba (sugarcane is its major produce).

156-092.r: Large coffee plantations of Brazil → Fazendas (coffee in the south-east; in colonial times sugar fazendas in the north-east).

156-093.r: Chad → petroleum; Niger → uranium; Rwanda → coffee; Benin → cotton (code 3 2 4 1).

156-094.r: Largest rice exporter in recent years → India, by quantity and value (FAO, 2013-23).

156-096.r: Commercial dairy farming → Denmark; commercial grain farming → Argentina; plantation farming → Malaysia; fruit production → France (code 3 1 4 2).

156-097.r: Not a major cocoa producer → Latvia; top cocoa producers (FAO 2024) → Cote d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Ghana; Cameroon 6th.

156-098.r: Two best-known largest cocoa producers → Cote d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast) and Ghana; FAO 2024 order: Cote d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Ghana, Ecuador, Nigeria.

156-099.r: Only 1 true: India has more arable land (153.87 million ha) than China (109.02). India's irrigated share is less than China's; statement 3 is also wrong.
156-099.c: The explanation calls India's per-hectare productivity higher than China's yet marks statement 3 wrong; China's average yield is in fact higher.

156-100.r: Both true: India has the largest cropland (168.32 million ha) vs USA (154.73), China (128.36), Japan (4.29); tropical monsoon climate allows varied crops all year.

156-101.r: Cereal yield → cereal produced per unit of harvested land (kg per hectare); not the total cereal production of a country.

156-102.r: Growing different crops in turn (crop rotation) keeps soil fertile, but neither assumption follows: a crop can be grown again in the same field; fertilizer may still be needed.

156-103.r: Not a Mediterranean agriculture area → Northern Australia; it is found in California, central Chile, south-western/southern Australia and SW South Africa (juicy fruits, grapes).

157-001.r: Coal → sedimentary rock (layered; holds fossils and mineral oil). Coal grades: anthracite (90-95% carbon) > bituminous (most abundant) > lignite (brown coal) > peat.
157-001.c: The book also lists slate and marble as sedimentary; both are metamorphic rocks.

157-002.r: Coal, crude oil and natural gas → fossil fuels, formed over millions of years from remains of living organisms.

157-003.r: All correct: China → leading coal producer; Donetsk Basin (Donbass) → Ukraine; Saar → Germany; Appalachian region (North Appalachian) → main US coal area.

157-005.r: Donetsk → Ukraine; Kuznetsk → Russia; Lancashire → U.K.; Saar → Germany (code 4 3 2 1).

157-006.r: Appalachian → USA; Lancashire → England; Ruhr → Germany; Kuzbass → Russia (code 4 1 2 3).

157-007.r: Largest hard coal reserves when asked → China; now (end of 2023) USA first, then Russia, China, Australia, India.

157-008.r: Largest coal centre of Ukraine → Donetsk (Donbas, eastern Ukraine), about 90% of its coal; other basins: Lviv-Volhynian, Dnieper (brown coal).

157-009.r: More than half of world coal → China and USA when asked; in 2023 China alone produced more than half (World Mineral Production).
157-009.c: The book gives no single answer (*): option (b) fitted when asked; now China alone gives over half.

157-010.r: Ruhr basin → famous industrial region of western Germany, on the Ruhr river; coal mines and industries.

157-011.r: Ruhr coalfield → Germany; gives the bulk of Germany's bituminous coal; steel and chemical industries, dense waterways and railways.

157-012.r: Largest coal reserves among options → China; top three coal reserves globally → USA, Russia, China.

157-013.r: Highest coal-producing country → China (2023, World Mineral Production).

157-014.r: Rukwa lake region (Tanzania) → coal (some mining); also gemstones like emerald, ruby, topaz, aquamarine.

157-015.r: Not a German coalfield → Lorraine Basin (mainly north-eastern France); Ruhr, Saar and Achen basins are in Germany.

157-016.r: Kuzbass (Russia) → rich in coal and iron ore; Novosibirsk is an important industrial centre. Both statements correct.

158-001.r: Earth's interior: iron is the most common metal, then nickel, then aluminium; crust: aluminium first, iron second. No nickel in options → aluminium.
158-001.t: Don't mix interior order (iron, nickel) with crust order (aluminium, iron).

158-002.r: Iron ore producers, descending, 2008: China > Brazil > Australia > Sweden; 2023: Australia > Brazil > India > China.

158-003.r: Largest gold producer in 2023 (and 2024) → China; Russia and Australia also among leaders.

158-004.r: Largest iron ore producer when asked → China; now (2023) Australia.

158-005.r: Marquette range (Marquette County, Michigan, USA) → iron ore.

158-006.r: Iron ore leaders (2019-23): Australia, Brazil, India, China; among the options (Philippines, America, Russia, India) → India.

158-007.r: Main iron ore producers of Europe → Russia, Ukraine, Sweden (2023: Russia, Sweden, Ukraine); France is not among them.
158-007.c: The book gives no single answer (*): France is in none of these ranks for iron ore; it was fifth in pig iron (2013).

158-008.r: Lorraine → France; Midland → U.K.; Kiruna → Sweden; Kostanay → Kazakhstan (code 4 3 1 2).

158-009.r: Placer gold on Ghana's coast has no source rock there; it came from gold-bearing veins of the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side.
158-009.c: BPSC's key is 'both true and R explains A', option (a) here. The book prints (b) and calls R 'not right', yet its own reasoning (Ghana's gold came from Brazil's veins when the continents were joined) supports (a).

158-010.r: Wrong pair: Germany – Normandy; Normandy is in France. Correct: Kazakhstan – Karaganda; Ukraine – Krivoy Rog; France – Pyrenees. Lorraine (France) → iron and steel.

158-012.r: Lake Superior region (North America) → iron ore reserves.

158-013.r: 'Rust Bowl' (Rust Belt) → iron and industrial region of north-eastern USA (Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania); includes Great Lakes and Pittsburgh regions → (e).

158-014.r: Great Lakes region of North America (USA and Canada's Ontario) → steel and engineering industries most developed.

158-015.r: Top three iron ore producers when asked → China, Russia, Australia; in 2023 → Australia, Brazil, India.

158-017.r: Minas Gerais (south-eastern Brazil) → high-quality iron ore; also manganese, tin, silver, zinc and precious stones.

159-001.r: Largest copper ore producer → Chile, then D.R. Congo and Peru (2023).

159-002.r: Copper leaders (2023): Chile, D.R. Congo, Peru; among Australia, China, India, USA → China.

159-003.r: Chile still leads copper output (2023) (A true) because it has the largest porphyry copper deposits in the Andes, e.g. Chuquicamata mine (R true, explains A).

159-004.r: Chile → largest copper producer (about 5372694 tonnes, 2023), as the Andes hold the largest porphyry copper deposits (A, R true; R explains A).

159-005.r: Zambia: rich copper belt (extending to Katanga, D.R. Congo) but slow progress → landlocked, no seaport, so exports suffer.

159-006.r: Japan → almost self-sufficient in copper (produces more than it consumes); not in bauxite, iron ore or mineral oil.

159-007.r: Largest copper producer of Africa when asked → Zambia; in 2023 → D.R. Congo.

160-001.r: Highest gold output among the options → China (375155 kg in 2023, World Mineral Production).

160-002.r: Gold output order when asked → South Africa > USA > Australia > China; in 2023 → China > Russia > Australia > Canada > USA.

160-003.r: Kalgoorlie and Coolgardie → gold mines of Western Australia; Australia has the world's largest gold reserves (Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

160-006.r: Johannesburg (largest city of South Africa, capital of Gauteng) → gold and diamond mining.

160-007.r: Largest gold exporter to India → Switzerland (projected for 2025).

160-008.r: Asia's biggest gold market when asked → Beijing, China; as of February 2026 → Shanghai Gold Exchange, China.

161-001.r: Largest silver producer → Mexico (2023), then China, Peru, Russia, Poland.

161-003.r: German silver (nickel silver) → copper alloy with nickel and zinc (usually 60% copper, 20% nickel, 20% zinc); named for its look, contains no silver.
161-003.t: Horn silver, ruby silver and lunar caustic do contain silver.

162-001.r: Odd one out → Bauxite (aluminium ore); haematite, magnetite and limonite are iron ores.

162-003.r: Largest aluminium producer when asked → USA; in 2023 → China (41594000 t), then Russia, India, Canada, UAE.

162-004.r: Aluminium producers (2023): China > Russia > India > Canada > UAE; among France, India, USA, Italy → India.

163-001.r: Tin → about 80% from placer deposits: gravity-concentrated heavy minerals near riverbeds, valleys and sea floor, spread in South East Asia.

163-002.r: Tin producers (2023): China, Indonesia, Myanmar, Peru, Brazil; China not in options → Indonesia.

164-001.r: Petroleum production, ascending, when asked: China, Iran, USA, Saudi Arabia; 2023 leaders: USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Canada, Iran.

164-002.r: Alaska → oil-producing US state; bought from Russia in 1867. Both statements correct.

164-003.r: Three leading petroleum producers (2023) → USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia.
164-003.c: When asked (2008), (c) Saudi Arabia, Russia, USA was the order; by 2023 data it is USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia, which no option gives.

164-004.r: Largest petroleum producer (2023) → USA, then Russia; among Kuwait, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Russia → Russia.

164-005.r: Middle East petroleum producers, descending (2023) → Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, UAE.
164-005.c: Among the four listed countries, the book's 2023 data give Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, then Kuwait, i.e. (b); UAE is simply not listed. When asked (2008), Kuwait out-produced Iraq, which fits (d).

164-006.r: All true: Middle East held over 60% of world oil reserves (when asked); Alaska's reserves about equal Texas; USA is a prominent producer and importer.

164-007.r: Largest petroleum producer of Southeast Asia → Indonesia (Sumatra, Java, Kalimantan).

164-008.r: Venezuela → major petroleum producer; oil gives over 80% of its export revenue (2025).

164-009.r: Largest proved crude oil reserves → Venezuela (303.2 billion barrels), then Saudi Arabia (267.2) (2024).

164-011.r: Largest oil reserves when asked (2006) → Saudi Arabia; now (2024) Venezuela (303.2 billion barrels) > Saudi Arabia > Iran.
164-011.t: Reserves leader is Venezuela; production leader is USA.

164-012.r: Largest oil reserves (2024): Venezuela, Saudi Arabia, Iran; among Kuwait, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria → Iran.

164-013.r: Highest petroleum producer of West Asia → Saudi Arabia; third in world after USA and Russia (2023).

164-014.r: Gasohol → unleaded gasoline (90%) + ethanol (10%); USA is the top producer and consumer (2024).

164-015.r: Brent crude → major crude oil classification and world benchmark price, sourced from the North Sea; light, with low (not zero) sulphur. Statements 1, 2 correct.

164-016.r: 'Peace Pipeline' → Iran–Pakistan (IP) gas pipeline; none of the given options.

164-017.r: Sumed (Suez-Mediterranean) pipeline, Egypt → Gulf of Suez (Red Sea) to Mediterranean near Alexandria; strategic alternative to Suez Canal for Persian Gulf oil to Europe.
164-017.t: Sumed carries crude oil only, not natural gas; the book notes (d) is possible literally, but takes (a).

164-018.r: First commercial oil well (1857) → Romania; 275 tonnes output officially recorded.

164-019.r: Group with a crop that cannot make biofuel → (c) Lentil, Sugarbeet, Wheat. Biofuel crops: sugarcane, corn, soyabean, rapeseed, jatropha.
164-019.c: The book says sugarbeet and wheat also cannot make biofuel; both are used for ethanol. Lentil is the crop that makes (c) right.

164-020.r: Top crude oil supplier to India in 2017-18 → Iraq (earlier Saudi Arabia; in 2025 Russia).

164-021.r: Ras Tanura refinery → Saudi Arabia, on the Persian Gulf coast near Jubail; started 1945.

164-022.r: Wrong pair: Kuwait – Kashagan; Kashagan oil and gas field is in Kazakhstan. Correct: Iran – Hafi Kel; Saudi Arabia – Dhahran; Iraq – Zubair.

164-023.r: Largest crude oil producer after USA → Russia (2023).

164-024.r: Pegu Yoma (low range between Irrawaddy and Sittaung rivers, Myanmar) → mineral oil.

165-001.r: Largest uranium producer (2023) → Kazakhstan, then Canada and Namibia; before 2009 Canada led (so 'prominent uranium/atomic minerals producer' → Canada).

165-004.r: Largest uranium reserves → Australia (2023); Olympic Dam mine in South Australia.

165-005.r: 'Uranium City' → Canada: northern Saskatchewan, near the north shore of Lake Athabasca.

165-006.r: Radium (Ra, radioactive) → extracted from pitchblende, a uranium ore.

165-007.r: Important uranium deposits among the options → Canada; biggest reserves now (2023) → Australia.

165-009.r: Not a major resource of Russia (when asked) → uranium; Russia is rich in iron ore, diamonds, gold, nickel, platinum. In 2023 Russia ranked 6th in uranium.

166-001.r: Seabed mining licences in international waters → UN International Seabed Authority (not Global Ocean Commission); India has such licences; rare earths lie on the seafloor. 2 and 3 correct.

166-002.r: Postmasburg and nearby areas (South Africa) → manganese.

166-003.r: Natural camphor → tree Cinnamomum camphora, native to China and Japan; in India from Blumea species; Borneo/Sumatra camphor from Dryobalanops.

166-004.r: Non-ferrous metals (negligible iron) → nickel, zinc, copper, aluminium (also tin, lead, titanium, gold, silver); iron ore, pig iron and steel are not.

166-005.r: Coal → Karaganda Basin; Gold → Highveld; Iron ore → Krivoi Rog; Mineral oil → San Joaquin Valley (code 2 1 4 3).

166-006.r: Mineral oil → Venezuela; Copper → Zambia; Manganese → Gabon; Bauxite → Guyana (code 3 1 4 2).

166-007.r: Wrong pair: Mesabi Range – copper; Mesabi → iron ore. Correct: Donbas Basin – coal; Mosul – petroleum; Transvaal – gold.

166-008.r: Iron ore → Mesabi (Lake Superior, USA); Petroleum → Baku (Azerbaijan); Copper → Bingham Canyon (Utah, USA); Uranium → Port Radium (Great Bear Lake, Canada).
166-008.h: Port Radium hints at radioactive minerals → uranium.

166-011.r: Correct pair → Copper – Arizona (USA); Coal – Karatzas, Iron ore – Rasatnoora and Petroleum – Donbas are wrong pairs.

166-012.r: Wrong pair: Saar – iron ore; Saar → coal. Correct: Kimberley – diamond; Witwatersrand – gold; Katanga – copper; Butte – silver.

166-014.r: Afghanistan's mineral find (worth $1 trillion), compared with Iran's oil-field discovery → lithium.

166-015.r: Leading titanium producer when asked → Russia; now (2025 data, USGS 2026) China leads titanium mineral concentrates.

166-016.r: Biggest bauxite producer → Australia (Indian Minerals Yearbook 2012); now (2025 data) Guinea is the major producer.

166-018.r: Chile is famous for → nitrate; largest natural source → Atacama Desert (north Chile, south Peru).

166-019.r: Bolivia → tin; Brazil → iron ore; Mexico → silver; natural nitrate → Chile (Atacama), so Peru–Nitrate is the wrongly matched pair.
166-019.c: The book calls all four pairs correct, but natural nitrate is Chile's (Atacama); Peru lost its nitrate fields (Tarapacá) to Chile in the War of the Pacific. So (d) Peru – Nitrate is the odd pair.

166-021.r: Rare earth worry: China, the largest producer (over 95% in 2010), restricted exports; demand for electronics rising. Wrong: they exist beyond China, Australia, Canada, Chile.
